Subdue
sub-DOO
v.
From Latin subducere / subdere, to bring under; sub- (under) + a root of leading or placing. To subdue is to bring a thing under ordered rule—the placing of something beneath a rightful authority.

Biblical Definition

Subdue means to bring under rule, and in Scripture it is first a mandate, not a conquest. God blesses the first pair and commands, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion (Gen 1:28)—spoken before the fall, so subduing is not a consequence of sin but part of the original vocation of the image-bearer. The earth is to be brought under ordered, fruitful cultivation by creatures who are themselves under God. The word then follows the pattern of redemptive history. God subdues nations under His people (Ps 47:3), and—far more importantly—subdues His people's worst enemy: he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea (Mic 7:19). Paul turns the mandate inward: I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway (1 Cor 9:27)—the man commissioned to subdue the earth must first subdue himself, and an unsubdued preacher is a disqualified one. The horizon is Christ's: He is able even to subdue all things unto himself (Phil 3:21). So the word runs in a straight line from Eden to the last day: creatures under God subdue the earth; sin resists; Christ subdues sin, death, and finally all things, and hands the kingdom to the Father.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SUBDUE as to conquer and bring into permanent subjection; to overpower; also to tame, to soften, and to bring land under cultivation.

expand to see more

SUBDUE, v.t. — To conquer by force or the exertion of superior power, and bring into permanent subjection; to reduce under dominion.

SUBDUE, v.t. — To overpower and destroy the force of; to tame; to soften; to subject to good order. Also, to break as land by plowing and harrowing, and render it mellow and fit for tillage.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:28 — "And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth."

Micah 7:19 — "He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea."

1 Corinthians 9:27 — "But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway."

Philippians 3:21 — "Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself."

Modern Corruption

The dominion mandate is read today either as a license for exploitation or as an embarrassment to be apologized for, and both misreadings skip the governing fact: the creature commanded to subdue is himself under God and answerable for how he rules.

expand to see more

One corruption treats subdue as a warrant for extraction: the earth as raw material, dominion as ownership without accounting. Scripture forecloses it. The subduer is a steward under a Lord who retains title—the earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof—and stewards give account. Webster's agricultural sense is the closest analogy the older language preserved: to subdue land is to plow and harrow it until it is mellow and fit for tillage. That is cultivation for fruitfulness, not strip-mining.

The opposite corruption treats the mandate itself as the problem—dominion recast as the root of ecological and colonial sin, with the ideal human as one who touches nothing and shapes nothing. That is not humility but abdication, and it leaves the world to be shaped by whoever feels no such scruple. Meanwhile the inward sense has been largely abandoned. Paul subdues his own body first, and a culture that regards appetite as identity has no category for the self-subduing man—which is why it produces so many who would remake the world and cannot govern their own evenings.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kabash, to bring into subjection or bondage; Greek hypotassō, to place under in ordered rank—dominion exercised by a creature who is himself under authority.

expand to see more

Hebrew kabash (H3533) — to subdue, bring into bondage, tread down; the verb of the creation mandate and of subduing land (Gen 1:28; Num 32:22, 29; Josh 18:1).

Greek hypotassō (G5293) — to place under, subject, subordinate in ordered rank; used of all things being subdued unto Christ (1 Cor 15:27-28; Phil 3:21; Heb 2:8).

Greek doulagōgeō (G1396) — to bring into slavery or subjection; Paul's word for what he does to his own body (1 Cor 9:27).

Usage

"Replenish the earth, and subdue it—a mandate given before the fall, not a consequence of it."

"He will subdue our iniquities—the enemy God most needs to subdue is inside His people."

"Paul subdues his own body first; an unsubdued preacher is a castaway."
